2027-01-25.title: Fourth Monday of Denha · Conversion of Saint Paul
2027-01-25.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: God calls Moses from the burning bush
He appeared also to me, as to one untimely born
2027-01-25.alt: Season of Denha. Conversion of St Paul. The Church Unity Octave concludes. Weekday readings of the day: Acts 16:25–34; Luke 5:12–16.
2027-01-25.verse: But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me has not been in vain. On the contrary, I worked harder than any of them—though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me.
theo: Today's readings set two great calls side by side. Moses, a fugitive shepherd in the desert, sees a bush that burns and is not consumed, and hears his name: “Moses, Moses!” God reveals himself: “I AM WHO I AM.” Saul, a zealous persecutor on the road, is thrown to the ground by a light from heaven and hears his name: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” He asks, “Who are you, Lord?” and hears: “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.” The God of the burning bush has a human face and a name, and he identifies himself with his suffering Church.

Saul is led blind into Damascus. Ananias, frightened but obedient, lays hands on him; “something like scales fell from his eyes, and his sight was restored.” He is baptized, and “immediately he began to proclaim Jesus in the synagogues, saying, ‘He is the Son of God.’” Years later Paul looks back with humility: Christ appeared to Cephas, to the Twelve, to more than five hundred, to James, “Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me. For I am the least of the apostles.” And then the great sentence: “by the grace of God I am what I am.”

The Gospel explains this grace. The owner of the vineyard hires workers at dawn, at nine, at noon, at three, and even at five o'clock, and pays them all the same. Those hired first grumble. He answers: “Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me? Or are you envious because I am generous?” Paul was hired at the eleventh hour, and received the full wage of grace. None of us earns salvation; all of us receive it. This is the good news for every latecomer, and the end of all envy in the Church.

The weekday readings carry the same grace further. In a Philippian prison at midnight Paul himself, the converted persecutor, is singing hymns when an earthquake opens the doors; the trembling jailer asks, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?”, and Paul answers, “Believe on the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.” That same night the whole family is baptized. In Luke a man covered with leprosy begs, “Lord, if you choose, you can make me clean”, and Jesus touches him: “I do choose. Be made clean.” The grace that met Saul on the road keeps finding the latecomers and the outcasts.
conn: “Moses, Moses” (Exodus 3:4) and “Saul, Saul” (Acts 9:4): the double name marks a decisive call.
The divine name revealed at the bush is echoed in Jesus' words, “I am Jesus” (Acts 9:5).
A sign of baptismal enlightenment; the early Church called Baptism “illumination”.
Paul's image for his late and unexpected call; grace overturns ordinary timing.
Workers hired at five o'clock receive a full day's wage; the Fathers saw here the Gentiles and late converts.
Ends today: the apostle who once divided now unites.
Acts 16:25–34 and Luke 5:12–16: the jailer of Philippi and the leper show the same unearned grace that called Saul.
altar: Paul's sight was restored, then he was baptized and ate (Acts 9:18–19). Baptism leads to the table of the Qurbana.
At the altar no one is paid by merit; all receive the same Lord, by grace.
outline: Ask: have you ever felt others got more than they deserved?

The householder hires at every hour: in childhood, youth, old age; no one should despair of being called.

The Church's commitment to Christian unity.
saints: Born in Tarsus, educated in Jerusalem, persecutor turned apostle, missionary to the nations, martyred in Rome.
2027-01-25.prayer: Lord God, you appeared to Moses in the burning bush and to Saul on the road to Damascus. By your grace make us what you want us to be, free us from envy at your generosity, and through the prayers of St Paul unite all Christians in one faith. Glory to you, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.

illus: A man from Changanassery was baptized at sixty-eight after years of mocking his wife's faith. At his first Communion he wept and said: I came at the eleventh hour, and the Lord gave me the full wage. His wife said: I prayed forty years; it was worth every day.

pm.open: Lord, you call us by name and give us grace we do not earn. Make us grateful and generous. Amen.
share: Moses, Moses! (Exodus 3:4). Do I hear God calling me by name?
Who are you, Lord? (Acts 9:5). Do I know Jesus personally?
Are you envious because I am generous? (Matthew 20:15). Where am I envious?
pm.resp: Lord, by your grace we are what we are.
interc: For the unity of Christians, at the end of the Unity Octave.
For those who persecute the Church.
For late converts and those returning to faith.
For our group, that we may rejoice in one another's gifts.
pm.close: Father, your grace is generous to all. Free us from envy and make us witnesses of your mercy. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, today two great calls are set side by side. Moses, a shepherd in the desert, sees a bush burning and not consumed, and hears: Moses, Moses! God reveals his name: I AM WHO I AM (Exodus 3:14).

Saul, on the road to Damascus, is thrown down by a light from heaven and hears: Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? He asks: who are you, Lord? The answer: I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting (Acts 9:4–5). The God of the burning bush now has a human face, and he suffers in his Church.
Blind, Saul is led into Damascus. Ananias lays hands on him; something like scales fall from his eyes; he is baptized, and immediately proclaims Jesus as the Son of God.
Years later Paul writes: last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me. And: by the grace of God I am what I am (1 Corinthians 15:8, 10).

The Gospel explains this grace. Workers hired at five o'clock receive the same wage as those hired at dawn. The owner says: are you envious because I am generous? (Matthew 20:15). Paul came late and received the full wage of grace.
None of us earns salvation; all of us receive it. Let us give thanks for grace, rejoice in others' blessings, and pray today that all Christians may be one. Amen.
kids: Children, St Paul started by hurting Christians, but Jesus changed him into his best messenger. God's love is for everyone, even people who come late!
Let us be happy when others get good things, because God is generous.

homily: Dear friends, today we celebrate the conversion of Paul. But there is another hero in the story, a quiet disciple in Damascus named Ananias.

The Lord said to him: get up and go to the street called Straight, and look for a man of Tarsus named Saul. Ananias answered honestly: Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints (Acts 9:11, 13). He was afraid, and he had good reason to be.

But the Lord said: go, for he is an instrument whom I have chosen to bring my name before Gentiles and kings (Acts 9:15). God sees what we cannot see. The man everyone feared was the man God had chosen.
So Ananias went, laid his hands on Saul and said: Brother Saul (Acts 9:17). His first word was brother. Something like scales fell from Saul's eyes, and he was baptised.

Who is the Saul in my life? The person I fear, avoid, or have given up on? Perhaps God is sending me, as he sent Ananias, to say: brother, sister. And let us bring that person to the Holy Qurbana in our prayer today. Amen.

intro: Saul did not change his zeal, his intelligence or his energy. He changed his centre. Conversion is not becoming someone else but becoming who God meant.

points.apply: Name one thing you are proud of and offer it to Christ.
Make a good confession this week.

sub: Faith in the Son of God who loved me.

concl: Conversion keeps our gifts but changes our centre.
Paul's zeal became love for Christ and for all peoples.
opts.resolve: Each morning this week I will pray Galatians 2:20: it is Christ who lives in me.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, what changed when Saul became Paul? Not his intelligence: he remained a brilliant scholar. Not his energy: he remained tireless. Not his zeal: he remained on fire. What changed was the centre of his life.

He writes: whatever gains I had, these I have come to regard as loss because of Christ (Philippians 3:7). His birth, his learning, his religious record, all the things he had been proud of, he now laid at the feet of Christ.

He discovered that if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation: everything old has passed away; see, everything has become new (2 Corinthians 5:17). This is what happens in every good confession: the old passes, the new begins.

And he could finally say: it is no longer I who live, but it is Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20).

God does not want to destroy our gifts but to set them on the right centre. Let us offer him our pride, make a good confession, and pray each day: Lord, live in me. And receive him in the Holy Qurbana as Paul's whole life. Amen.

intro: Theme: “By the grace of God I am what I am.”

He fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?”

points.apply: Treat the Church as the Body of Christ.

But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me has not been in vain. On the contrary, I worked harder than any of them—though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me.
